_comment: Preguntas ORIGINALES tipo NIE del capítulo 3.1. No son preguntas reales del examen. Comprueba con tu edición 2027.

questions.scenario: Which is the correct definition of theft under s. 1 Theft Act 1968?
options: Dishonestly appropriating property belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it

questions.scenario: RAY swaps the price label on a television for a cheaper one in a shop. He is stopped before reaching the till. Has he 'appropriated' the TV?
options: No, because he has not left the shop
No, because he has not paid
Yes – assuming any of the rights of an owner is an appropriation
Only if he damages the label

questions.scenario: An elderly man, of sound mind, gives his carer £20,000 as a valid gift. The carer knew he was being exploited. Can this be theft?
options: No, a valid gift can never be theft
Yes – a valid gift can be an appropriation; dishonesty is the key question
Only if the man lacked capacity
Only if the carer used force

questions.scenario: A con artist persuades a victim to hand over money by lying. The victim consents to the transfer. Is there an appropriation?
options: Only if the money is cash
Yes – consent, even if obtained by deception, does not prevent appropriation

questions.scenario: Which belief, if honestly held, means the appropriation is NOT dishonest under s. 2(1)?
options: I thought the shop was too expensive
I believed I had the legal right to take it
explanations: s. 2(2): willingness to pay doesn't stop dishonesty.

questions.scenario: ANNA takes a sandwich from a shop and leaves the exact price on the counter because the till queue is long. The shop has a clear 'pay at the till' rule. Which is correct?
options: Her appropriation may be dishonest even though she was willing to pay (s. 2(2)); dishonesty is decided on Ivey
She cannot be dishonest because she paid
She commits making off without payment
She has no intention to permanently deprive
explanations: She intended to keep the sandwich.

questions.scenario: Must a belief under s. 2(1) be reasonable?
options: Only if the defendant is an adult
No – it only needs to be honestly held

questions.scenario: ZOE finds a ring in the street. She keeps it, honestly believing the owner cannot be found by taking reasonable steps. Is she dishonest?
options: Yes, she must hand it in
explanations: Not a legal requirement for s. 2.

questions.scenario: Which of these is NOT 'property' capable of being stolen under s. 4?
options: A credit balance in a bank account

questions.scenario: LEO picks wild mushrooms in a wood to cook for his family. Is this theft?
options: Yes, if the land is private
No – picking wild mushrooms is not theft unless for reward, sale or other commercial purpose
Only if he uses a knife

questions.scenario: The same LEO picks wild mushrooms to sell to a restaurant. Which is correct?
options: It can be theft because it is for sale/commercial purpose

questions.scenario: Electricity is used dishonestly by bypassing a meter. Which offence?
explanations: Electricity is not property for theft.

questions.scenario: SAM's car is at a garage for repairs. The garage is entitled to keep it until paid. SAM secretly takes it back at night without paying, intending never to pay. Can SAM steal his own car?
options: No, nobody can steal their own property
Only if the car is financed
Yes – property belongs to anyone with possession, control or a proprietary interest (s. 5(1))
Only if he damages the garage

questions.scenario: MEG's employer overpays her salary by mistake. She realises and spends it, intending not to repay. Which subsection makes the money 'belong to another'?
explanations: Correct: got by mistake with obligation to restore.
Obligation to deal in a particular way.

questions.scenario: A charity collector keeps some of the cash collected for the charity. Which subsection is most relevant?
options: s. 5(3) – property received under an obligation to deal with it in a particular way

questions.scenario: LLOYD borrows films from a cinema, copies them and returns them a few hours later undamaged. Is there an intention to permanently deprive?
options: No – the films were returned with their goodness and virtue intact
Yes, because borrowing is always theft
Only if he sold the copies
explanations: Copying does not take the 'goodness' of the reels.
Not the test for theft of the reels.

questions.scenario: A student takes a classmate's monthly bus pass, uses it until it expires, and then returns it. Which is correct?
options: There may be ITPD because borrowing in circumstances equivalent to an outright taking (value exhausted) counts (s. 6)
No ITPD because it was returned

questions.scenario: Teenagers take a car without the owner's consent, drive it around and abandon it intact. Which is the most appropriate offence?
explanations: ITPD may be hard to prove.

questions.scenario: After taking a car without consent, the driver crashes into a wall, damaging the wall. Which offence becomes available?
Is TWOC (s. 12) a summary or indictable offence?
A diner eats a meal and leaves without paying, intending never to pay. Which offence is most suitable?
options: Making off without payment (Theft Act 1978, s. 3)
explanations: Ownership may have passed – making off is designed for this.

questions.scenario: Which element is required for making off without payment?
options: Knowing payment on the spot is required and intending to avoid payment

questions.scenario: A man is stopped in the street, away from his home, with a screwdriver and gloves he intends to use to break into cars to steal. Which offence?
explanations: Correct: not at place of abode, article for theft/burglary.

questions.scenario: Can a person be guilty of going equipped while at their own home?
options: No – the offence requires the person not to be at their place of abode
explanations: Not necessarily (a vehicle can be a place of abode in some cases ⚠).
questions.manualRef: Blackstone's 2027 · 3.1 · Going equipped – place of abode

questions.scenario: A visitor removes a painting displayed in a public gallery, intending to return it later. Which offence may apply even without ITPD?
options: s. 11 – removal of articles from places open to the public

questions.scenario: A person buys a bike in good faith for a fair price. Later he learns it was stolen and keeps it. Is keeping it theft?
options: No – s. 3(2) protects a good-faith purchaser for value

questions.scenario: A person finds a wallet and initially intends to hand it in. Two days later he decides to keep the money. Has he appropriated it?
options: No, because he got it innocently
Yes – a later assumption of rights by keeping it as owner can be an appropriation
Only if the owner sees him

questions.scenario: What is the maximum sentence for theft on indictment (⚠ check edition)?
A wild deer in a forest is shot and taken by a poacher. Is the deer 'property' for theft?
options: Yes, if the land is private
Generally not, unless tamed/kept or already reduced into someone's possession (s. 4(4))

questions.scenario: Which mental element distinguishes theft from TWOC?
explanations: Theft needs dishonesty, but the key difference is ITPD.
